https://www.politico.eu/article/emmanuel.text: PARIS — The international space summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday and Thursday was meant to show that Europe is getting serious about investing in its space sector. But the two-day gathering under the glass dome of Paris’ Grand Palais ended up demonstrating that Europeans are not spending enough to cut reliance on the U.S. to access space — at least not yet. On the sidelines of the summit, space companies from around the world announced billions in new partnerships and investments, but the big get-together fell short of the public funding announcements needed to access space without U.S. help. Advertisement Advertisement Things had already started to look bad a few days before the summit when American space companies such as SpaceX decided to ditch the event after White House pressure , accusing France of “anti-competitive practices” and disregarding the perspectives of U.S. industry. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also skipped the event, despite it being co-chaired by France and Germany. French officials downplayed the importance of the U.S. absence, stressing that the summit would provide Europe with an opportunity to step up its game on space. But several participants said that the summit's goals were unclear and that it lacked political commitments from countries other than France to boost public investment in the space sector. Good idea, bad execution “I had mixed feelings,” said Ezequiel Sánchez, the executive president of PLD Space, one of the companies selected by the European Space Agency to develop European launchers. “We were all expecting the rabbit out of the hat,” said Sánchez, noting that the summit was “a good idea,” but with a “bad implementation.” The lack of public funding comparable to the levels delivered by the U.S. loomed large at the summit. Advertisement Advertisement On Wednesday evening, Josef Aschbacher, the director general of the European Space Agency, urged European countries to boost funding to the ESA. In a meeting with ministers from ESA member states, he said that by investing €1 billion per year over the next 10 years, Europe could finally afford to send astronauts into space without relying on NASA. “It is up to you. Will we be passengers or pilots?” Aschbacher told ministers. One space official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, said that the countries looked at the proposal with interest, which still needs to be discussed at an ESA ministerial meeting in Rome in December. “It is no miracle that the U.S. has a company like SpaceX. It is because the public sector is investing a lot,” the official said. On the first day of the summit, the space industry associations of France, Germany and Italy urged the EU to allocate “at least €60 billion” to the sector as part of its upcoming 2028-2034 budget. Speaking after Macron at the summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed that under the Commission's proposal, €131 billion would be allocated to defense, security and space. Macron, meanwhile, called for autonomous European space missions in the coming years, backed by "a European space budget that matches our ambitions" — without quantifying the sums involved. Advertisement Advertisement Even if there were no new public funding announcements in Paris, the summit delivered three technical declarations — on the Copernicus program , on space-based scientific data and on the allocation of radio satellite frequencies — as well as making a broader call for a more ambitious European space policy. Other participants interpreted the fact that few heads of state and government showed up as a sign that they did not fully back Macron’s initiative. “The main partners didn’t really buy in,” said one space policy insider, pointing to the absence of Merz and of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and calling the summit “the swan song of French leadership.” The Italian and German governments were, however, represented at the ministerial level and several space deals with France and Italy were announced during the summit. Gilles Rabin, a former official at France’s space agency CNES and now an independent consultant, said that Macron’s diplomatic efforts were also undermined by the fact that he will leave power next year, as he can’t run for a third mandate. “This summit represents Macron’s final wishes regarding space, his European testament,” he said. https://www.warringtonguardian.co.uk/new.text: Business Food and drink Leisure Warrington Meet the business bringing a taste of Hungary to Warrington Business Food and drink Leisure Warrington By Tabitha Wilson Reporter Share 0 Comments Cheshire Chimney Cake sells a range of delicious Hungarian dishes (Image: Supplied) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. THERE'S no shortage of fantastic independent businesses across Warrington. For this week's Business of the Week, Madarasi-Pap told us all about Cheshire Chimney Cake. If you would like your business to feature as Business or Trader of the Week, email tabitha.wilson@newsquest.co.uk What’s your full name? Madarasi-Pap Tamás What’s the name of the business? Cheshire Chimney Cake What’s the address? Unit 1, John Street, Warrington, WA2 7UB (inside the Hungarian Sausage grocery shop) Are you the owner/manager? Owner When did you open the business? The physical store opened in Jun 2020 in a joint venture with the 'Hungarian Sausage' grocery shop, where people can get fresh Hungarian delicacies like chorizo, cured meat, palinka, and ingredients for Hungarian dishes like 'Gulyas'. Has it always been in the same location? Yes, we are located near the train station, and we also have free customer parking behind the shop. Are you local to the area? Did you grow up here? No, I'm afraid. I live in Southport, but Warrington is a central Hub for the community. It's a busy spot, easy to reach by all motorways. We have customers from as far as Birmingham, Kendal, Leeds, and Chester. Tell me a bit about your business. What do you do? I offer an authentic Hungarian street food experience. You can enjoy a delicious bite to eat while browsing a wide selection of traditional Hungarian products and groceries in the shop. What services do you provide? I make the famous Hungarian street food specialties freshly: Chimney Cake, Langos with different toppings (Hungarian deep-fried pizza), Kolbasz (baked giant seasoned sausage), Hungarian style Burger and famous mini bread: 'Kifli'. For example, Chimney Cake is a 400-year-old traditional wedding cake; it could be described as a Hungarian doughnut, but instead of frying, I'm baking it in a rotisserie oven, and it will be super light and fluffy on the inside but with a crunchy caramel layer on the outside, topped with vanilla, walnut, cinnamon, or other flavours. Langos (pronounce it: 'LAHN-gosh') yeast-based dough that is deep-fried until it is golden brown and crispy on the outside while remaining soft and chewy on the inside. Traditionally, it is served hot and rubbed with garlic, then topped with sour cream and grated cheese. Modern variations can range from simple salted versions to loaded toppings like pulled pork or gyros style. I also serve the infamous 'Kolbasz,' which is a giant baked, perfectly spiced Hungarian smoked sausage, homemade by the shop itself. Why did you decide to open your own business? My original passion was to introduce Hungarian cuisine here in England, and I wanted to challenge myself. What’s your business background? I had no business background, but I built it step by step, from baking at home to market stalls to a fixed location over the last nearly 9 years. Why this type of business? I always had a passion for creating something that other people can enjoy and to make a lasting experience/memory. What makes your business different from others in the same area/field? Simple. Made with love and enthusiasm from the first flour drop till the final creations. I make everything as if I would make it for myself or for my family, maintaining a 5-star food hygiene rating since opening. What sets your business apart from your competitors? Unique experience, flavours, and texture in Hungarian style. Why do loyal customers return to your business? I would separate this into two groups. People who have never had it before can enjoy flavours that no other cuisine can provide, and for people who grew up on this street food, it brings back childhood memories with that homely feeling. What’s next? What do the next few months hold for you and your business? I would like to introduce our Hungarian street food venture and shop to a wider audience. Due to our growing popularity, we kindly recommend placing your pre-orders at least one day in advance, particularly for visits over the weekend. https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text: Walter Koenig in Star Trek. Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Walter Koenig in Star Trek. Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty Images Star Trek Walter Koenig, actor best known as Chekov on Star Trek, dies aged 90 The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writer Adrian Horton Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.18 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Walter Koenig, the actor known for playing Pavel Chekov throughout the Star Trek franchise, has died, his representative confirmed to the Hollywood Reporter . He was 90. Koenig died at his home in North Hollywood surrounded by his daughter and niece, according to a Facebook post by Zachery McGinnis, the founder of Galactic Productions, an appearance agency that counted the actor as one of its clients. His death was attributed to “old age”, with no other details provided. “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world,” McGinnis wrote. “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.” The post concluded: “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.” “My heart is heavy,” wrote Koenig’s Star Trek co-star George Takei on Facebook on Monday. Takei first met Koenig in the 1960s, “on the bridge of the Enterprise” and remained friends for six decades; Koenig served as Takei’s best man at his wedding in 2008. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend,” Takei wrote. “To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.” Jesse Thorn, the host of the NPR show Bullseye, also confirmed the news on Bluesky , citing his friend Danielle Koenig, the late actor’s daughter. “Something I was struck by knowing Danielle, her husband and her late brother Andrew (and talking with George Takei) was the very sincere love those Star Trek cast members had for each other,” he wrote. “That whole thing was thrust upon them and their obvious deep friendship was so clear. What a gift.” Born in Chicago but raised in Manhattan as the child of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig began his acting career in 1962, with an uncredited role as a sentry in Combat!. He joined Star Trek for the start of the second season and appeared in 36 of the 50 episodes that aired between 1967 and 1969. He continued his role as the Russian Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies derived from the show, released between 1979 and 1991, as well as in a two-part crowdsourced Renegades series that debuted online in 2017. He most recently reprised the voice of Chekov in a 2023 episode of the animated series Star Trek: Picard. Koenig also worked as a writer, penning episodes for such series as The Powers of Matthew Star, Family, Land of the Lost and The Incredible Hulk. He wrote, produced and starred in the 2010 sci-film InAlienable, starring Richard Hatch. Koenig was married to the actor Judy Levitt, with whom he appeared in three Star Trek movies as well as another acclaimed sci-fi series, Babylon 5, which ran from 1994 until 1998. The couple were together from 1965 until her death in December 2022 at the age of 83. Their son Andrew, who played Richard “Boner” Stabone in the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died in 2010 at age 41. Koenig is survived by his daughter, the actor and screenwriter Danielle Koenig.
